narrative.text: Acknowledges those who coordinated and contributed to the 2022 guidelines on tuberculosis in children and adolescents, led by the WHO Global Tuberculosis Programme. It lists the Guideline Development Group members with their institutions, along with reviewers, observers and the systematic review teams. Funding for the update came from Unitaid and USAID.
The list of abbreviations used in the guidelines on tuberculosis in children and adolescents.

Defines terms used in the guidelines, such as active case-finding, adherence, advanced HIV disease, adverse events and age groups from infant to adolescent. Many further definitions cover diagnostic, treatment, drug-resistance and outcome terms. Definitions apply to this document and may differ elsewhere. The section ends with references, including WHO consultations on outcome definitions.

Summarises the 2022 guidelines, noting that about 1.1 million children fall ill with tuberculosis each year and fewer than half are notified, with low uptake of preventive treatment among young contacts. It sets out global targets, the rationale for updating the 2014 guidance, the objectives and the target audience. It lists the eight new recommendations, including Xpert Ultra as the first test on several specimen types, treatment decision algorithms, a 4-month regimen for non-severe tuberculosis, bedaquiline and delamanid for young children with drug-resistant tuberculosis and a 6-month regimen for tuberculous meningitis. A table of consolidated existing recommendations follows, covering areas such as HIV care, nutrition and contact investigation.

Gives the background to the guidelines, noting the burden of tuberculosis in children and young adolescents, the case detection gap due to diagnostic difficulties and the 24% fall in child notifications in 2020 linked to COVID-19. It also mentions low preventive treatment coverage and explains that this update brings all relevant recommendations together in one guideline.
Explains that new research since the 2014 WHO guidance on childhood tuberculosis prompted a review and update, with new and existing recommendations brought together in one consolidated guideline.

States the guidelines' objectives: to give evidence-based recommendations across the cascade of care for children and adolescents and to help cut tuberculosis illness and death in line with global targets.
Identifies the target audience as tuberculosis, primary care, maternal and child health and AIDS programmes, clinicians, and civil society and implementing partners.

Explains that the 2022 WHO consolidated guidelines on managing TB in children and adolescents combine new evidence-based recommendations, relevant recommendations from other WHO TB guidelines since 2014 and some unchanged 2014 recommendations. It notes that source wording and age definitions are kept and points users to the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform and web annexes.

Sets the scope of the guideline update, defining children as under 10 and adolescents as 10–19 years, and uses the cascade of care from TB exposure to treatment outcome as its analytical framework, shown in a figure. It lists the PICO questions addressed, on diagnosis, treatment and models of care such as decentralized and family-centred integrated services. Two background questions concern the socioeconomic impact of TB on families and how best to engage adolescents in care.

Describes how the guidelines will be published on the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform and disseminated through webinars, training and technical support, and lists the age-disaggregated indicators that will be monitored. It states that the recommendations will be reviewed within five years, and the interim recommendation on treatment decision algorithms within two years.

Outlines the structure of the 2022 guidelines chapter by chapter, from the introduction through screening and contact investigation, prevention, diagnosis and treatment to care of children with TB and HIV or malnutrition. It notes which chapters contain new recommendations and that the final chapter sets out research priorities.

Opens chapter 2 by consolidating existing WHO recommendations on TB screening and contact investigation relevant to children and adolescents. Table 3 lists recommendations such as systematically screening household contacts and people living with HIV, and HIV counselling and testing of contacts depending on HIV prevalence.

Consolidates WHO recommendations on TB prevention relevant to children and adolescents, drawn from guidelines on infection prevention and control, the BCG vaccine position paper and guidelines on TB preventive treatment. Table 4 lists measures such as triage and respiratory isolation of people with TB symptoms, BCG vaccination, testing for TB infection and preventive treatment regimens. Recommendations on preventive therapy for people living with HIV, including 36 months of isoniazid in high-transmission settings, close the section.

Describes the gap in TB diagnosis among children, with only about a third of an estimated 1.1 million cases notified in 2020 and most deaths occurring in under-fives who never received treatment. It explains causes such as paucibacillary disease, lack of a sensitive point-of-care test, sampling difficulties and limited primary care capacity, and notes a 2021 expert consultation advising that intrathoracic lymph node TB be classified as pulmonary TB.

Recommends Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra as the initial test for pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance in children using sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate, gastric aspirate or stool, instead of smear microscopy, culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing. It sets out the justification and evidence, noting the limited sensitivity of the earlier Xpert MTB/RIF assay among children and people with HIV. Implementation considerations cover acceptability and feasibility of specimen collection, and monitoring advice covers laboratory registers and reporting notifications by five-year age group.

Gives an interim conditional recommendation that integrated treatment decision algorithms may be used to diagnose pulmonary TB in children under 10 with presumptive TB, while still seeking bacteriological confirmation where possible. It explains that new algorithms are detailed in the operational handbook and that the recommendation will be reviewed after 24 months. The section covers the evidence, the need to suspect drug-resistant TB where relevant, and monitoring of treatment response and outcomes.

Table 5 consolidates WHO recommendations on TB diagnostics relevant to children and adolescents, including Xpert MTB/RIF and Ultra as initial tests on various specimen types and molecular tests for detecting drug resistance. It notes that adults in the source guidelines include adolescents aged 15 and over, and states that commercial serodiagnostic tests should not be used for children. The page ends with the opening of chapter 5 on treatment.

Introduces the treatment chapter, listing four new recommendations: a four-month regimen for non-severe drug-susceptible TB, a six-month intensive regimen for TB meningitis, and bedaquiline and delamanid for children of all ages with MDR/RR-TB. It notes the source guidelines from which other treatment recommendations are consolidated.

Recommends a four-month regimen for children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB, defining non-severe disease and advising the standard six-month regimen for others. It notes ethambutol should be added in settings with high HIV or isoniazid resistance prevalence. The justification cites potential benefits of shorter treatment for costs, toxicity, drug interactions and adherence. Implementation considerations stress accurate classification of severity and follow-up for up to 12 months after treatment to detect relapse.

Gives a conditional recommendation that a six-month intensive regimen of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethionamide may be used as an alternative to the 12-month regimen for TB meningitis in children and adolescents without drug resistance. It notes the 12-month regimen remains an option and that the shorter regimen should not be used in those living with HIV owing to lack of data. Evidence, diagnostic considerations and monitoring of uptake and outcomes are also covered.

Addresses treatment of MDR/RR-TB in children, noting an estimated 25 000–32 000 cases a year but only a few thousand started on second-line treatment, with numbers falling during COVID-19. It presents the recommendation on bedaquiline for children of all ages, explaining that earlier advice applied only from age 6 because of limited pharmacokinetic and safety data in younger children. It then covers delamanid for children of all ages within longer regimens. Implementation and monitoring points include the risk of delamanid resistance, cardiac and neuropsychiatric safety monitoring, and recording treatment outcomes.

Reproduces, in Table 6 of WHO's consolidated guidelines on managing tuberculosis in children and adolescents (Module 5), existing WHO recommendations on TB treatment for this age group. These cover regimens for drug-susceptible pulmonary, peripheral lymph node, osteoarticular and meningeal TB, with dosing advice for young infants and the 4-month rifapentine–moxifloxacin regimen from age 12. It also lists recommendations for isoniazid-resistant and multidrug- or rifampicin-resistant TB, ending with notes on treatment monitoring by sputum testing.

Introduces the chapter on models of TB care for case detection and preventive treatment in children and adolescents, noting two new recommendations and other consolidated ones on patient support. It describes how paediatric TB capacity is often centralised, primary care staff lack confidence and many chances for contact tracing and prevention are missed, which frames the questions on decentralised and family-centred care.

Sets out two new conditional recommendations, based on very low certainty evidence, that decentralised and family-centred, integrated models of care are options for delivering TB services to children and adolescents with TB symptoms or exposure. Remarks clarify that decentralisation strengthens services at lower levels rather than replacing specialist care, and should target areas with poor access or high prevalence. The section then presents the justification and evidence and implementation considerations, including differentiated service delivery. It ends with monitoring and evaluation advice on planning, registers, sex-disaggregated data and service quality.

Table 7 lists WHO recommendations on care and support during TB treatment that apply to children and adolescents, including health education, adherence interventions such as tracers, material and psychological support, and community- or home-based and video-supported treatment options. Footnotes explain what each type of support involves.

Opens the chapter on special situations, covering WHO recommendations for TB in children and adolescents with HIV or malnutrition and feeding of infants of mothers with TB. Table 8 gathers recommendations on HIV testing, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, antiretroviral therapy eligibility and timing, and TB/HIV care. It also includes nutritional recommendations, such as managing severe acute malnutrition, and ends with a note on pyridoxine with isoniazid.

Lists research gaps identified by the guideline development group, grouped by topic such as TB screening, diagnostic approaches and treatment decision algorithms. The priorities call for studies on screening tools for different age groups, validation and implementation of diagnostic algorithms, and research on community perceptions and the quality of TB diagnosis in children.
The reference list for the guideline (127 items), citing mainly WHO TB reports and guidelines and studies on childhood tuberculosis.

Annex 1 lists the WHO guidelines and position papers whose recommendations are incorporated into this module, covering screening, contact investigation, infection control, BCG, preventive treatment, diagnosis, treatment, HIV and nutrition.

A long annex table comparing each recommendation in WHO's 2014 guidance on managing TB in children with its current status in this module. For each item it gives the original wording and source, whether it was updated, kept, copied to the operational handbook or replaced, and the new wording. Topics include Xpert MTB/RIF and Ultra diagnostic testing, treatment regimens, preventive therapy, HIV and reporting age bands, which change to 0–4, 5–9, 10–14 and 15–19 years. It also lists the new interim recommendation on treatment decision algorithms and ends with WHO Global TB Programme contact details.
The front matter of the WHO consolidated tuberculosis guidelines, Module 5 on managing tuberculosis in children and adolescents (2022), with ISBNs, licence terms, contents and links to web annexes.
